blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Distribution-matching distillation enables high-quality image generation in only a few denoising steps. However, distilled student models often map different initial noise samples to similar outputs under the same prompt. To locate where diversity is lost, we compare the teacher and student along the sampling trajectory. The largest measured reduction in the response to different initial noises occurs during the first, high-noise step. When we replace the first step with the teacher's corresponding trajectory and leave the final three student steps unchanged, most of the output diversity returns. This suggests that the first step is a key point for restoring diversity. Motivated by this finding, we introduce \emph{ReSeed}, a post-distillation method that adds a seed-response bias adapter only to the first student step and aligns its velocity with the teacher's first-interval secant velocity. All student weights and later denoising steps remain unchanged. We evaluate ReSeed on three text-to-image models (SD3-Medium, SD3.5-Medium, and FLUX.1-dev) and one text-to-video model (Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B). For a distilled 4-step FLUX.1-dev model, \emph{ReSeed} requires only $0.00196\%$ additional trainable parameters relative to the base model and is trained on 8,000 prompt--noise pairs, while keeping the distilled student fully frozen and requiring no target images, perceptual losses, or adversarial losses. It improves DINO diversity by $48.3\%$ while maintaining competitive visual quality. These results show that substantial diversity can be recovered through a lightweight, data-efficient tuning of only the first denoising step, without finetuning the full student model.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Diffusion and flow models generate high-quality images and videos, but often
require many network evaluations [ Ho et al., 2020 , Esser et al., 2024 ] .
Distillation reduces this cost by training a student to generate samples in
only a few denoising steps [ Salimans and Ho, 2022 , Song et al., 2023 , Yin et al., 2024b ] . However, students trained with distribution
matching distillation (DMD) often produce similar outputs from different
initial noises under the same prompt. This loss of diversity reduces the
range of results that users can obtain from a few-step model.

Previous works try to address this problem by aligning the student’s response
to initial noise [ Huang et al., 2026 ] , assigning different training objectives
to early and late denoising steps [ Wu et al., 2026 ] , or using the base model
for the first sampling step [ Gandikota and Bau, 2025 ] . These studies
highlight the importance of preserving variation during early generation. Further related work is discussed in 6 .
Building on these findings, we ask a practical question: can we recover diversity in an already distilled student by changing
only its first denoising step, while keeping its original weights and later
steps fixed?

We first examine this question through controlled interventions on
SD3-Medium. We replace the first student step with the teacher’s trajectory
over the same time interval, then run the final three student steps without
any changes. This yields a higher DINOv3 diversity than that of the 28-step teacher.
The result shows that the
unchanged later steps can preserve much of the diversity recovered by the
teacher’s first interval. It supports our central hypothesis: a substantial
part of the measured diversity loss can be restored at the first step,
without retraining the rest of the student.

blocks.en:
Motivated by this finding, we introduce ReSeed , a post-distillation
method that trains small bias adapters only for the first student step
(Figure 3 ). We add learned per-channel biases to
transformer block outputs and keep all original student weights frozen.
Training matches the student’s first-step velocity to the teacher’s average
velocity over the same interval, using the same prompt and initial noise.
Matching these velocities also matches the states reached at the first
student boundary. At inference, the biases are enabled only during the
first step; later steps use the unchanged student, with no teacher calls
or additional denoising steps.
The biases are shared across prompts and noise seeds, so they do not
provide new seed-specific information. Instead, the frozen nonlinear
network turns the shared biases into input-dependent corrections.
Our analysis links diversity recovery to better alignment with the
teacher’s seed-dependent responses, rather than simply increasing
response magnitudes. This explains why we study a small first-step
correction instead of changing the entire sampling process.

blocks.en: Our main contributions are: • Most diversity loss occurs in the first denoising step. We show that most of the diversity loss in few-step distilled models occurs in the first denoising step, while the frozen suffix retains the ability to preserve diversity. • A small first-step adapter can recover lost diversity. We introduce ReSeed , a first-step residual tuning that restores lost diversity while keeping the pretrained distilled student frozen, requiring less than 0.005 % 0.005\% additional trainable parameters and approximately 8,000 prompt–noise pairs. • Existing distilled models can be repaired without repeating distillation. Our results demonstrate that diversity in an already distilled model can be substantially improved through a lightweight post-hoc tuning, without repeating distillation or fine-tuning the whole original student. This provides a practical way to enhance the diversity of existing few-step generative models after training.

blocks.en:
Reduced sample diversity is a known cost of these
methods. Score-identity
distillation studies guidance-dependent diversity and introduces zero- and
anti-guidance objectives [ Zhou et al., 2025 ] ; GAD matches initial-noise
Jacobian–vector products during training [ Huang et al., 2026 ] . At the sampler
level, Gandikota and Bau [2025] trace part of the loss to premature
structural commitment and recover diversity by using the multi-step base model
for the first denoising step. At the training-schedule level, DP-DMD gives that
step a teacher-derived target-prediction objective while retaining DMD later [ Wu et al., 2026 ] , and 1.x-Distill separates coarse distribution matching from
detail refinement [ Li et al., 2026 ] . Data-Forcing Distillation instead
performs a short post-training correction using teacher scores on real video
samples [ Chen et al., 2026 ] . CADS improves diversity at inference by
adding noise to the conditioning signal and gradually reducing it during
sampling [ Sadat et al., 2024 ] . ReSeed differs in both question and mechanism:
it diagnoses an already distilled, frozen image generator and changes only the first step of the frozen student without target images, adversarial training, or a
teacher call at inference. We use finite differences only for diagnosis. Vendi
is an alternative set-level diversity summary [ Friedman and Dieng, 2023 ] .

blocks.en: 7 Discussion & Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 讨论和结论

blocks.en:
ReSeed repairs the first denoising step of a distilled student while leaving
the later steps unchanged. It adds small residual biases to the frozen
denoiser and trains them to match the teacher’s average velocity over the
first high-noise interval. At inference, the biases act only in step 1, so
steps 2–4 use the original student. Training needs no target images or
videos. On SD3-Medium, SD3.5-Medium,
and SenseFlow-FLUX, the adapters add only 0.002 0.002 – 0.004 % 0.004\% denoiser
parameters and raise DINOv3 diversity by 37.1 % 37.1\% , 39.3 % 39.3\% , and 48.3 % 48.3\% ,
respectively, while lowering FID. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B DMD2, 300 updates
raise video-level DINOv2 diversity by 27.1 % 27.1\% , recovering 56.2 % 56.2\% of the
measured teacher–student gap. ReSeed thus provides a low-cost
post-distillation correction without retraining the student.

blocks.en:

use flow-matching transformers; we have not tested non-flow-matching diffusion
models or U-Net backbones, so it remains unclear whether the same first-step
behavior holds for those models.

blocks.en:
In summary, Proposition 1 identifies what the
regression objective controls, and Proposition 2 explains how shared internal biases can change seed differences.
The observed link to final-image diversity comes from the matched evaluations
above and the teacher-prefix intervention, not from either proposition alone.
